title_original: The Distance Between Being There and Being Seen at La Biennale di Venezia
excerpt_original: Just because you are invited into the room does not mean you decide where you stand. Suzette Bell-Roberts 8 October 2026 At La Biennale di Venezia, visibility has its own geography, and not every country […]

blocks.text: Just because you are invited into the room does not mean you decide where you stand.

At La Biennale di Venezia, visibility has its own geography, and not every country enters it on equal terms. For African and global African diaspora pavilions, the question is not simply who is present, but who gets seen, how they are seen, and what determines the difference. The Senegalese Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

blocks.caption: The Senegalese Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

blocks.text: At La Biennale di Venezia, some countries have the privilege of being discovered; others have to persuade you to look for them. Walk through the Giardini and the Arsenale and national pavilions appear one after another, introducing visitors to artists and art histories they may never have intended to see. Beyond these venues, discovery becomes less assured. Some pavilions remain on routes visitors naturally take, while others require a conscious decision to find them. This creates a hierarchy of attention: some countries benefit from passing visitors, while others depend on visitors who already know enough to seek them out.

For countries whose artists and art histories have been marginalised by Western-dominated narratives of art history, this matters. Venice offers an opportunity to challenge that imbalance and bring their own histories to new audiences. But participation alone cannot guarantee that their pavilions will be encountered, that their artists will receive meaningful attention, or that greater visibility will continue beyond the Biennale.
Here, the geography of visibility begins.

In 2026, one hundred countries are taking part: twenty-nine at the Giardini, twenty-five at the Arsenale and forty-six elsewhere in Venice. Seven nations are exhibiting for the first time, four of them from Africa: Guinea, Equatorial Guinea, Sierra Leone and Somalia. Although these countries have the same official status, their situations regarding access, attention, and representation differ.

Egypt’s Silence Pavilion: Between the Tangible and the Intangible , by Armen Agop, and Brazil’s Comigo ninguém pode , by Rosana Paulino and Adriana Varejão, occupy permanent pavilions in the Giardini, while Morocco’s Asǝṭṭa , by Amina Agueznay, is located in the Arsenale. South Africa too has a long-term presence at the Arsenale, even though it did not take part this year. These locations sit within the routes where Biennale attention is already concentrated, allowing visitors to encounter the pavilions without deliberately seeking them out. Countries without permanent sites face a different challenge: they must establish their presence elsewhere in Venice and attract visitors to a location that may change with each participation. Permanent pavilions also acquire familiarity over time, becoming part of the geography returning visitors already know, while countries that move between venues must make themselves visible in a new place each time. Egyptian artist Armen Agop outside the Egyptian Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

blocks.caption: Egyptian artist Armen Agop outside the Egyptian Pavilion.  Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

blocks.text: A pavilion situated outside the Giardini or the Arsenale doesn’t necessarily mean it is peripheral. Senegal’s WURUS and Uganda’s Kampala are in adjacent locations right on the Riva degli Schiavoni. Cuba’s Hombres Libres / Free Men , which is on Via Garibaldi, is also in a similar position along the main pedestrian route leading to the Giardini and the Arsenale. The Democratic Republic of the Congo’s first pavilion, Simba Moto! Seize the Fire! Saisis le feu!, is also conveniently located on a busy square in Castello. These pavilions sit along paths Biennale visitors are likely to follow and can therefore see without having to look for them specifically.

Guinea’s first National Participation, Le Son de l’Art: l’Écho de la Matière , occupies a very different geography. Located on the island of San Servolo, it cannot be reached simply by turning down another Venetian street. Visitors have to decide to go there, allow time for the journey and pay for a vaporetto, turning a pavilion visit into a destination in itself.

Mere proximity can also be misleading. The exhibitions Ethiopia’s Shapes of Silence , by Tegene Kunbi and curated by Abebaw Ayalew, and Zimbabwe’s Second Nature | Manyonga , curated by Fadzai Veronica Muchemwa, were both held at Castello, near the Giardini, Arsenale, Senegal, and Uganda. Yet finding them revealed how easily visibility can change within a few metres. Official Biennale signage on the Riva degli Schiavoni directed visitors down the alley towards both Ethiopia and Zimbabwe, but where the route divided, only Ethiopia was clearly signposted. We had deliberately set out to visit both and still struggled to find Zimbabwe. On a map, the difference was negligible; on foot, a missing sign made one pavilion considerably easier to find than the other.

Financial resources also shape visibility. Countries without permanent pavilions must secure temporary venues, often long before the Biennale opens, so budget size and timing can determine which spaces remain available. Funding can influence the kind of art that can be brought to Venice and exhibited, as well as the resources available for communications and for artists and curators to be present during the crucial opening days. The consequences are visible throughout: in where a pavilion is located, what audiences encounter when they arrive, who is there to speak about the work and how effectively the exhibition attracts attention beyond its doors.

ART AFRICA encountered the consequences firsthand. We were in Venice specifically to report on the African and global African diaspora pavilions, yet received no communication from Haiti, Tanzania, Uganda, Guinea, or New Guinea: no press releases, invitations, or approaches to arrange interviews. We then repeatedly emailed the media contacts listed for these pavilions in the official press material from La Biennale di Venezia, but received no response and, months later, still have not heard from them. The Cuban Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

blocks.caption: The Cuban Pavilion. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

blocks.text: We cannot know why, nor does this mean that these pavilions received no publicity elsewhere. But if specialist media actively seeking to cover them could not make contact through the official channels provided, how effectively were they reaching audiences who did not already know they were there?

But visibility is only one part of the question. Once a pavilion has been found, another issue remains: who has been chosen to represent the country, who made those choices, and what version of the country is being made visible? Sierra Leone, Guinea, Somalia and Equatorial Guinea, all participating for the first time, bring these questions into sharp focus.

Sierra Leone’s first participation makes this question particularly relevant. Mondi Presenti / Worlds of Today , curated by Italians Sandro Orlandi Stagl and Willy Montini, brings together sixteen artists: four from Sierra Leone, four from other ECOWAS countries (the Economic Community of West African States)—Senegal, Togo, Benin, and Nigeria—seven from Italy, and one from Mexico. The curatorial statement places the pavilion within the context of ECOWAS while also referring to a history of exchange between Africa and Italy. The inclusion of artists from neighbouring West African countries therefore clearly relates to that framework. Less clear is why seven Italian artists make up almost half of Sierra Leone’s first national presentation, how the Mexican artist fits within the curatorial concept, and ultimately who determines the version of Sierra Leone that enters the Biennale’s official record.

Guinea’s inaugural Le Son de l’Art: l’Écho de la Matière , curated by Italian curator Carlo Stragapede, raises the stakes further. The exhibition brings together roughly 66 artists, including a significant number of Italians, while only a small minority appear to be Guinean. The issue is not simply who was selected, but what informed those choices and how such a large international exhibition comes to represent Guinea on its first national platform at the Biennale. Whose understanding of the country and its contemporary cultural community is being presented in its name?

Also participating for the first time, Equatorial Guinea’s The Forest The Undergrowth , curated by Catalan curator Joan Abelló, makes the issue even more explicit. Its 23 exhibitors include artists from Italy, Spain, China, Romania, Finland, Albania, Cameroon, Cyprus, Germany and Israel, alongside only one clearly identified Equatoguinean artist, Fernando Nguema Madja. The pavilion also includes Catalan-born Modest Gené Roig, who lived and worked in Equatorial Guinea. Here the question of representation has already been challenged from within the country’s cultural community. Before the Biennale opened, a group of Equatoguinean cultural practitioners publicly argued that contemporary voices from the country were largely absent and called for local artists and cultural professionals to be included in the curatorial process. The Giardini. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

blocks.caption: The Giardini. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

blocks.text: Somalia’s first National Participation has prompted an even more direct debate over who gets to represent a country in Venice. SADDEXLEEY , featuring Ayan Farah, Asmaa Jama and Warsan Shire, is curated by Stockholm-based Mohamed Mire and Italian project manager Fabio Scrivanti. The Somali Arts Foundation has publicly criticised the pavilion for what it describes as a lack of meaningful consultation with artists and arts organisations based in Somalia, while the Somali collective Warbixinta Cidda has called for Scrivanti’s removal, questioning the appointment of an Italian co-curator given Italy’s colonial history in Somalia. An open letter subsequently drew on both statements and called for a boycott if its demands were not addressed. The dispute adds another dimension to the question of representation: not simply which artists are selected, but who is consulted, who participates in making those decisions and whose understanding of the country is ultimately presented in its name.

Taken together, these four inaugural pavilions raise a broader question of curatorial authority. The issue is not the curator’s nationality, nor must an African national pavilion be curated by someone from that country or continent. What matters is who has the authority to represent a country, what knowledge and relationships inform their choices, how its artists and cultural practitioners participate in that process, and ultimately who determines what becomes visible in the country’s name.

These questions are nothing new; the Kenya pavilion of 2013, curated by two Italians, included eight Chinese artists, one Italian, and two Kenyans. When comparable concerns were raised about the country’s representation in 2015, Kenyan artists objected, and the government then withdrew its support. The first Namibian pavilion in 2022, A Bridge to the Desert , also attracted similar criticism. Curated by Italian Marco Furio Ferrario and featuring the anonymous artist RENN, this exhibition drew objections from Namibia’s arts community over the country’s representation; the Namibian government subsequently withdrew its support, although the exhibition took place.

The controversies showed the difference between official participation and cultural legitimacy; a national pavilion makes visible not only a country but a specific representation of it, so it matters as much who has the authority to construct that representation as it does that the country is seen at all. The Bahamas Pavilion, installation view. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts.

blocks.caption: The Bahamas Pavilion, installation view. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts.

blocks.text: Visibility is also influenced by the professional networks that come together in Venice, particularly during the opening week, when museum directors, curators, collectors, foundations, galleries, and the press stay for a few intense days; having an established relationship with an artist, a curator, or an institution can help make a pavilion into a destination, while those who do not have such connections depend more on drawing attention outside of their current networks.

For journalists, those few days are often the only chance to interview artists and curators while in Venice, since time is limited and the city is expensive. So many events compete for attention—namely the Giardini, the Arsenale, the 100 National Participations, the collateral events, and the various exhibitions—that harder-to-find pavilions must put in extra time and effort. Moreover, geography and professional networks can interact: a pavilion off the main routes must work harder to enter the channels through which professional attention flows.

Yet a pavilion’s audience is not limited to the people who walk through its doors. Media coverage can take an exhibition far beyond Venice, reaching readers and viewers who will never attend the Biennale. Reviews, interviews, photographs, videos, podcasts, newsletters and specialist publications can introduce artists and their work to entirely new audiences, while an interview might bring an artist to the attention of a curator who never saw the exhibition in Venice. This coverage also gives the pavilion life beyond the months of the Biennale, creating a record that can circulate long after the exhibition has closed. In this sense, what happens beyond the pavilion can become as important as what happens inside it.

International media coverage is not necessarily more valuable than national, regional, or specialist coverage, which can offer the backgrounds and contexts that general reporting tends to ignore. What matters is how far the coverage reaches, whether it introduces the artists and their work to people who were not already familiar with them, and whether the attention results in anything beyond Venice.
Being highly visible doesn’t necessarily mean having a real impact. Image courtesy of Brendon Bell-Roberts

It is important when considering the reasons why countries choose to invest in Venice, since taking part requires a great deal of financial and institutional resources and therefore high numbers of visitors do not necessarily indicate that the investment has been worthwhile; a pavilion that is crowded may bring about some degree of exposure without achieving any real results, while fewer interactions could result in exhibitions, acquisitions, commissions, publications, or in the establishment of long-term institutional relationships.
No single criterion can judge success, since there shouldn’t be one. However, participation alone cannot measure success.

If international exposure is one reason for taking part in the Biennale, then more significant questions arise once the pavilion has opened. Has it brought the artists and their respective art histories to the attention of people who are not already familiar with them? Has anyone written about, interviewed, or exhibited their work in other institutional contexts? Have the artists obtained new opportunities? Have any relationships persisted after Venice?

The geographical aspect of visibility therefore extends beyond Venice; it affects the chances of discovery, directs professional interest, shapes the kind of content linked to a country’s name, and influences how far that representation will extend afterwards.

For African countries and the global African diaspora, the stakes are particularly high. La Biennale di Venezia can bring artists and art histories long marginalised by Western-dominated narratives to wider attention, opening doors to audiences, institutions and conversations that might otherwise remain out of reach. But an official place within the Biennale does not guarantee an equal chance of being discovered, nor does it necessarily give artists and cultural communities greater authority over how their countries and histories are presented.
The differences begin long before the doors open and can continue long after they close.
Presence, then, is only the beginning. If nobody was looking for you, did Venice make them look — and when they did, who decided what they would see?
